excerpts.text: **Susumu Kitagawa**, **Richard Robson** and **Omar Yaghi** are awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2025. They have developed a new form of molecular architecture. In their constructions, metal ions function as cornerstones that are linked by long organic (carbon-based) molecules. Together, the metal ions and molecules are organised to form crystals that contain large cavities. These porous materials are called metal–organic frameworks (MOF). By varying the building blocks used in the MOFs, chemists can design them to capture and store specific substances. MOFs can also drive chemical reactions or conduct electricity.

excerpts.text: [This morning’s Nobel Prize in Chemistry](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2025/press-release/) is one that’s been [anticipated](https://cen.acs.org/people/nobel-prize/win-2024-Nobel-Prize-Chemistry/102/web/2024/09) for several years now: it goes to [Susumu Kitagawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susumu_Kitagawa) of Kyoto, [Richard Robson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Robson_(chemist)) of Melbourne, and [Omar Yaghi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omar_M._Yaghi) of Berkeley for [metal-organic frameworks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metal%E2%80%93organic_framework).

The [“scientific information” document](https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2025/10/advanced-chemistryprize2025.pdf) at the Nobel site does a good job with the history of the MOF field. Metal-organic frameworks took until the late 1980s to be realized, and it’s Robson who gets the credit there.

Kitagawa and Yaghi were early workers in the field, and there was certainly a lot to work on.

Kitagawa demonstrated that particular MOFs could adsorb particular gas molecules (once the solvent had been removed from the cavities) and that this process was reversible.

Among Yaghi’s contributions has been the synthesis of some extremely stable MOFs using zirconium and other elements, things which are impervious to water and can be heated to hundreds of degrees without falling apart, which has led to a lot of interest from the chemical industry for catalytic applications. (Zirconium MOFs themselves were first described in 2008 from Peter Lillerud at Oslo).
